findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State the concurrency assumption for offset files (single-instance systemd invocation, or add a per-file lock) and confirm the read-to-write window widening introduced by publishing-before-writing is safe.
evidence: Offset files are shared state read at start and written at end of each block
Reordering the write to after put-metric-data increases the read-to-write interval
Plan does not mention single-instance/systemd exclusivity or file locking
findings.finding: The plan reorders offset writes to occur after the CloudWatch publish but does not state whether offset files can be written by concurrent script invocations; moving the write after a network call widens the window between read and write, and no locking/single-instance assumption is documented.
findings.location: Repair plan — 'the matching offset advances only after a successful CloudWatch call'
scenarios: Two overlapping observability.sh runs (e.g. a slow AWS call causing overlap with the next timer tick) both read the same offset, one publishes and advances, the other re-publishes an overlapping delta or clobbers the offset
findings.suggested_fix: Add a sentence documenting that observability.sh runs single-instance under systemd (or add flock around each offset read/publish/write), and note it in the reliability preservation bullet.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add a one-line positive rationale for the deferred-offset reorder (e.g. 'the count is re-derived from the cumulative grep every run, so leaving the offset unadvanced on a failed publish is sufficient to recover the delta on the next successful run — no buffering/retry state is needed').
evidence: Plan states the fix ('Reorder each of the six concrete publish shapes so the matching offset advances only after a successful CloudWatch call') but gives no rationale for choosing reorder over a buffer/retry design.
G6(4): absence of a positive rationale for the chosen approach is a finding; a rejected-alternatives section is NOT required.
findings.finding: The plan specifies the reorder mechanism and its constraints thoroughly but does not state a POSITIVE rationale for why the deferred-offset reorder is the right approach over alternatives (e.g. buffering/retrying unacked deltas). Because the count is re-derivable from the cumulative grep on the next run, a simple reorder recovers losslessly without added state — but the plan never articulates this 'why it fits' justification.
findings.suggested_fix: In the Repair plan, prepend a rationale sentence: because each stream recomputes `total` from the full cumulative grep on every run, not advancing the offset on a failed publish is sufficient to republish the accumulated delta on the next successful run — making the minimal reorder loss-free without any extra buffering or retry state.
